title: Ingress & Ingress Controllers
summary: Route outside HTTP(S) traffic to Services by host and path, pick a controller with IngressClass, and terminate TLS.

blocks.text: Visitors from the city arrive at the **main port gate** (Ingress). A receptionist reads each visitor's host name and path and sends them to the right port phone number (Service), which forwards to bays. The gate only takes web visitors (HTTP and HTTPS); other traffic needs a `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` entrance. Posting the rules alone does nothing without a receptionist on duty. The port now recommends the newer gate system (Gateway API), and this gate's rulebook is frozen.
An Ingress is an API object (`networking.k8s.io/v1`) that manages **external access to Services**, typically HTTP. Rules on the Ingress decide which Service gets each request.

steps.text: HTTP and HTTPS traffic from outside the cluster reaches an **Ingress controller**. An Ingress has no effect without one.
The **Ingress** resource holds the routing rules, hosts and paths, that the controller applies.
A matching request goes to the rule's backend **Service**, which forwards it to its Pods.

items: It can give Services externally reachable URLs, load balance, terminate SSL/TLS and do **name-based virtual hosting**.
It handles **HTTP and HTTPS only**. It does not expose arbitrary ports or protocols. For other traffic use a Service of type `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`.
An **Ingress controller** fulfils the Ingress, usually with a load balancer. Creating only the Ingress resource **has no effect**.

blocks.text: The Kubernetes project **recommends Gateway API instead of Ingress**. The Ingress API is **frozen**: it stays GA with no plans for removal, but it gets no further changes.

The gate's rulebook needs someone to follow it: a **receptionist agency** (the Ingress controller) that you hire and set up yourself. The port maintains the AWS and GCE agencies; many outside ones exist, such as NGINX, Traefik and HAProxy. You may hire several at once, so each rulebook names its agency with `ingressClassName`, pointing to an IngressClass. Each agency works a little differently, so read its handbook.
An Ingress only works if an ingress controller is **running in the cluster**. You choose at least one and set it up yourself.

items: The Kubernetes project itself supports and maintains the **AWS** and **GCE** ingress controllers.
Many third-party controllers exist, for example the NGINX Ingress Controller, Traefik, HAProxy, Contour (Envoy-based) and Istio Ingress.
You can run **any number** of controllers. Each Ingress picks one by setting `ingressClassName` to the `.metadata.name` of an IngressClass.
`ingressClassName` replaces the older annotation method.
Controllers behave slightly differently, so read your controller's docs for its caveats.

sections.heading: The Ingress resource and its rules

blocks.text: A rulebook page (the Ingress resource) says: visitors for this host and this path go to that port phone number (`service.name` plus a port). Both host and path must match. Leave the host blank and the rule covers every web visitor at the gate. A path can instead point to another kind of desk in the same yard (`resource`), but never to both. Agencies may also read sticky notes (annotations) for extras.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: <ingress-name>
spec:
  ingressClassName: <class-name>
  rules:
  - host: <host>            # optional
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /<path>
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: <service-name>
            port:
              number: <port>

items: **host** is optional. With no host, the rule applies to all inbound HTTP traffic on the controller's IP.
Each **path** has a backend: `service.name` plus `service.port.name` or `service.port.number`.
Both host and path must match before traffic goes to the backend.
A backend can instead be a **resource** (an ObjectRef to another object in the same namespace, such as a CRD). `resource` and `service` are mutually exclusive; setting both fails validation.
Controllers often read **annotations** for extra behaviour. Which ones depends on the controller.
The Ingress name must be a valid DNS subdomain name.

blocks.text: Every path rule must say how strictly to compare (`pathType`). **Exact** wants the whole path, letter for letter. **Prefix** compares folder by folder, so `/foo/bar` covers `/foo/bar/baz` but not `/foo/barbaz`. **ImplementationSpecific** leaves it to the agency. When several rules fit, the longest path wins, and on a tie Exact beats Prefix. A wildcard host covers one extra name label only: `bar.foo.com` fits, `baz.bar.foo.com` does not.
Every path **must** have a `pathType`; a path without one fails validation.

rows: The whole URL path, case sensitive. `/foo` does not match `/foo/`
Element by element, split on `/`, case sensitive. `/foo/bar` matches `/foo/bar/baz` but not `/foo/barbaz`
Up to the IngressClass; may act like Prefix, Exact or something else

items: Trailing slashes are ignored for Prefix: `/aaa/bbb/` matches a request for `/aaa/bbb`.
When several paths match, the **longest path wins**. On a tie, **Exact beats Prefix**.
Hosts can be exact (`foo.bar.com`) or wildcard (`*.foo.com`). A wildcard covers **one DNS label only**: `bar.foo.com` matches, but `baz.bar.foo.com` and `foo.com` do not.

blocks.text: Each agency registers a **port-wide agency card** (IngressClass, always cluster-scoped) naming who runs it (`.spec.controller`) and, optionally, where its extra settings live (`.spec.parameters`). One card can be stamped "default" with the `is-default-class` annotation, and rulebooks that name no agency get it. Stamp two cards default and the front desk turns away new rulebooks with no `ingressClassName`. The old `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` sticky note is replaced.
An **IngressClass** names the controller that implements it (`.spec.controller`) and can point at extra config through `.spec.parameters`. The IngressClass API is always **cluster-scoped**.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: <class-name>
  annotations:
    ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
spec:
  controller: <controller-name>

items: `.spec.parameters.scope` is `Cluster` (the default) or `Namespace`. With `Namespace` you must also set the `namespace` field inside `.spec.parameters`.
New Ingresses without `ingressClassName` get the class annotated `ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"`.
Before 1.18, classes were set with the `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation. It was never formally defined; `ingressClassName` replaces it but is not an exact equivalent.

blocks.text: If **more than one** IngressClass is marked default, the admission controller rejects new Ingresses that have no `ingressClassName`. Keep at most one default.

sections.heading: Default backend, fanout and virtual hosts

blocks.text: Some rulebooks have no rules at all, just a fallback desk (`.spec.defaultBackend`) for every visitor; when the rules list is empty, that fallback is required. One host can fan out by path to several port numbers, saving entrances. Or several host names can share one gate, sorted by the name the visitor asks for. To change a live rulebook, edit it with your radio (`kubectl edit ingress`) and the agency reconfigures.

items: **`.spec.defaultBackend`** handles requests that match no rule. If `.spec.rules` is empty, `.spec.defaultBackend` is **required**. If it isn't set, unmatched requests are handled however the controller decides.
**Single Service:** an Ingress with only a default backend and no rules.
**Simple fanout:** one host, several paths, each to a different Service. Keeps the number of load balancers down.
**Name-based virtual hosting:** several `host` rules on the same IP, routed by the Host header. A rule with no host catches everything else.

blocks.text:
kubectl apply -f <ingress.yaml>
kubectl get ingress <ingress-name>        # ADDRESS may show <pending> for a minute or two
kubectl describe ingress <ingress-name>   # rules, backends, default backend
kubectl edit ingress <ingress-name>       # e.g. add a new host

To change a live Ingress, use `kubectl edit ingress <name>` (or `kubectl replace -f` with a modified file), then confirm with `kubectl describe ingress <name>`. The controller reconfigures the load balancer when the object changes.

For secure visitors, the receptionist keeps a sealed envelope (a `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret holding `tls.crt` and `tls.key`) and checks credentials at the gate, on door 443 only. Past the gate, visitors walk to the bays unescorted (plaintext). Several secure host names can share door 443 if the agency supports SNI. The catch-all rule gets no secure check, so each secure host must match a named host rule.
Secure an Ingress by referencing a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/tls` whose keys are **`tls.crt`** and **`tls.key`**.

spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
      - <host>
    secretName: <tls-secret-name>
  rules:
  - host: <host>          # must match the tls host
    http: ...

items: Ingress supports a **single TLS port, 443**, and terminates TLS at the ingress point. Traffic to the Service and Pods is plaintext.
Different TLS hosts share port 443 using **SNI**, if the controller supports it.
TLS does not work on the default (host-less) rule, so `tls` hosts must explicitly match hosts in `rules`.
TLS features vary between controllers.
Advanced load balancing (persistent sessions, dynamic weights) is not exposed through Ingress. Health checks aren't either; readiness probes give a similar result.

flashcards.front: Which protocols does an Ingress route?
flashcards.back: HTTP and HTTPS only. Other traffic needs a NodePort or LoadBalancer Service.

flashcards.front: What happens if you create an Ingress but no controller is running?
flashcards.back: Nothing. The Ingress resource on its own has no effect.

flashcards.front: Which ingress controllers does the Kubernetes project itself maintain?

flashcards.back: Exact, Prefix, ImplementationSpecific. A path without a pathType fails validation.

flashcards.front: Two paths both match a request. Which wins?
flashcards.back: The longest matching path. If still tied, Exact beats Prefix.
No. A wildcard covers a single DNS label only.

flashcards.front: Annotation that makes an IngressClass the cluster default?
Key names required in an Ingress TLS Secret?
Which port does Ingress TLS use, and where is TLS terminated?
flashcards.back: A single port, 443. TLS ends at the ingress point; traffic to the Service is plaintext.

flashcards.front: Ingress vs Gateway API: what does the Kubernetes project recommend?
flashcards.back: Gateway API. The Ingress API is frozen: still GA, not being removed, but no further changes.

flashcards.front: Is the IngressClass API namespaced or cluster-scoped?
flashcards.back: Always cluster-scoped. Only its parameters can be namespaced (scope: Namespace).

questions.stem: You apply a valid Ingress to a fresh cluster but nothing routes traffic. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: No Ingress controller is running in the cluster
options.explanation: An Ingress needs a controller to satisfy it; the resource alone has no effect.

options.text: The backend Service is of type ClusterIP
options.explanation: Ingress backends are ordinary Services; nothing on the page requires another type.

options.text: The rule has no host field
options.explanation: host is optional; without it the rule applies to all inbound HTTP traffic.

options.text: The Ingress has no tls section
options.explanation: TLS is optional; plain HTTP Ingresses work without it.

questions.stem: You need to expose a non-HTTP TCP service to the internet. What does the Ingress page suggest?

options.text: A Service of type NodePort or LoadBalancer
options.explanation: Ingress handles only HTTP/HTTPS; other protocols typically use NodePort or LoadBalancer Services.
pathType changes path matching only; Ingress still only routes HTTP(S).

options.text: An Ingress with a tls section on port 443
options.explanation: TLS on Ingress is still HTTPS, not arbitrary TCP.
Scope controls where class parameters live, not which protocols are supported.

questions.stem: An Ingress path is `/foo` with pathType Exact. Which request matches?

options.explanation: Exact matches the full path exactly and case sensitively.
The docs' table shows Exact /foo does not match /foo/.
Subpaths only match with Prefix.
Exact matching is case sensitive.

questions.stem: An Ingress has path `/aaa/bbb` with pathType Prefix. Which requests match? Select 2.

options.explanation: Prefix matches subpaths element by element.
Prefix matches the trailing slash.
Prefix is not a string prefix; bbbxyz is a different path element.
The request is shorter than the rule path, so /aaa/bbb is not a prefix of it.

questions.stem: Paths `/foo` (Prefix) and `/foo` (Exact) both exist. A request for `/foo` arrives. Which is used?

options.explanation: Equal-length matches prefer the Exact path type over Prefix.
On a tie, Exact has precedence.
Precedence is by longest path, then path type, not by order.
The default backend is only used when nothing matches.

questions.stem: An Ingress rule for host `*.foo.com` matches a request with Host header `foo.com`.

options.explanation: The wildcard covers exactly one DNS label, so foo.com does not match.
Correct: only hosts like bar.foo.com match *.foo.com.

questions.stem: A cluster has two IngressClasses annotated as default. A user creates an Ingress without ingressClassName. What happens?

options.text: The admission controller prevents the Ingress from being created
options.explanation: With more than one default IngressClass, new Ingresses lacking ingressClassName are blocked.

options.text: The oldest default class is assigned
options.explanation: No tie-break exists; creation is prevented.
The Ingress is not created at all.

options.text: The Ingress is created with no class and ignored
options.explanation: The admission controller rejects it instead.

questions.stem: Which statements about Ingress TLS are correct? Select 3.

options.text: The Secret must contain keys tls.crt and tls.key
options.explanation: Those are the required key names.

options.text: Ingress supports a single TLS port, 443
options.explanation: The page states only port 443 is supported.

options.text: TLS is terminated at the ingress point
options.explanation: Traffic from the ingress to the Service and Pods is plaintext.

options.text: TLS works on the default rule with no host
options.explanation: TLS won't work on the default rule; tls hosts must match rule hosts.

questions.stem: You run two ingress controllers. How does an Ingress choose which one implements it?

options.text: Set spec.ingressClassName to the name of an IngressClass
options.explanation: ingressClassName references the IngressClass's .metadata.name.

options.text: Set spec.defaultBackend to the controller's Service
options.explanation: defaultBackend handles unmatched requests; it does not pick a controller.

options.text: Set pathType to the controller name
options.explanation: pathType only accepts Exact, Prefix or ImplementationSpecific.

options.text: Only one ingress controller may run per cluster
options.explanation: You may deploy any number of ingress controllers.

questions.stem: The Kubernetes project plans to remove the Ingress API now that Gateway API exists.

options.explanation: The page says there are no plans to remove Ingress; it is frozen, not deprecated for removal.
Correct: Ingress stays GA but gets no further changes; Gateway is recommended.

questions.stem: An Ingress has no `.spec.rules`. Which field must it set?

options.explanation: Without rules, all traffic goes to the default backend, so it is required.
TLS is always optional.
It can be omitted when a default IngressClass exists.
parameters is a field of IngressClass, not Ingress.

questions.stem: A backend specifies both `service` and `resource`. What happens?

options.explanation: Resource and Service are mutually exclusive in a backend.

options.text: The service is used and resource is ignored
options.explanation: There is no fallback; both together is invalid.
Ingress doesn't expose weighting; the combination is rejected.

options.text: The resource takes precedence over the service
options.explanation: Neither wins; specifying both fails validation.

questions.stem: You must add a new host rule to an existing Ingress named `web` in place. Which command fits?

options.explanation: The page updates an Ingress by editing it, then checks with kubectl describe.
describe shows the rules but doesn't change them.
get only lists the Ingress and its address.
